name: Phoenix
keyDiscovery: Directly scooped and confirmed subsurface water ice on Mars, discovered perchlorate oxidizers and calcium carbonate in arctic soil, and detected snow falling from cirrus clouds.
missionLegacy: Proved that vast reservoirs of accessible water ice exist only centimetres beneath the Martian soil, revolutionizing our understanding of water habitability and resources on Mars.
funFact: Phoenix watched dice-sized chunks of white material excavated from the 'Dodo-Goldilocks' trench vanish over four sols — direct visual proof that the material was water ice sublimating into the dry air.
heritageNote: Phoenix rests in the polygon-patterned arctic permafrost of Vastitas Borealis; during the dark polar winter of 2009, heavy dry-ice carbon dioxide frost completely encased the lander.

objects.name: Phoenix Polar Lander
objects.description: A three-legged pulsed-thruster lander built from flight-proven hardware from the Mars Surveyor 2001 program. It used soft-pulsed monopropellant hydrazine thrusters rather than airbags to touch down gently without disturbing delicate subsurface ice.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Confirmed that the polygon ground patterns observed from orbit are thermal contraction cracks created by deep subsurface permafrost ice expanding and contracting.
objects.legacy: Operated for 161 days in the harsh Martian arctic, exceeding its 90-day prime mission before the sun dropped below the horizon.
objects.firstPerson: They named me Phoenix because I rose from the ashes of cancelled missions. I flew to the far north of Mars, where the ground cracked in giant stone polygons. When my rockets fell silent, my cameras looked down and saw pure white ice just below my feet.

objects.name: Robotic Trenching Arm & Rasp
objects.description: A 2.35-metre articulated robotic arm made of titanium and carbon composite, equipped with a backhoe scoop, a tungsten-carbide rasp, and a thermal and electrical conductivity probe (TECP). It dug trenches up to 18 cm deep.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Excavated the 'Snow White' and 'Dodo-Goldilocks' trenches, exposing pure white water-ice sheets 5 centimetres below the regolith.
objects.legacy: First machine to directly touch and scrape extraterrestrial water ice, delivering ice shavings into laboratory ovens.
objects.firstPerson: My titanium scoop bit into the frozen arctic soil with a metallic screech. Five centimetres down, my teeth struck hard, glittering white ice. I scraped its shavings and watched them melt in our onboard beakers. I touched Martian water with my own hands.

objects.name: TEGA Thermal Gas Analyzer
objects.description: An array of eight single-use miniature vacuum ovens paired with a magnetic-sector mass spectrometer. The ovens heated soil and ice samples up to 1,000°C to measure the vaporized gases released at specific mineral decomposition temperatures.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Detected water vapor liberated at 0°C and carbon dioxide released at 725°C, confirming the presence of calcium carbonate (chalk) formed in liquid water.
objects.legacy: Demonstrated that the Martian arctic once experienced liquid water that reacted with carbon dioxide in a warmer, thicker ancient climate.
objects.firstPerson: I was a cluster of eight tiny kilns in the freezing arctic. When the arm poured ice shavings past my motorized doors, I sealed my chamber and cranked my coils to a thousand degrees. Steam puffed into my spectrometer — undeniable, sweet Martian water vapor.

objects.name: MECA Wet Chemistry Cell & AFM
objects.description: The Microscopy, Electrochemistry, and Conductivity Analyzer included four single-use wet-chemistry beakers filled with Earth water and reagents, optical and atomic force microscopes, and ion-selective electrodes.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Discovered perchlorates (ClO4-) at 0.5% concentration in the soil and measured a mildly alkaline pH of 7.7, comparable to terrestrial asparagus-friendly soil.
objects.legacy: The discovery of perchlorates explained the puzzling 1976 Viking GCMS results and fundamentally altered understanding of Mars organic chemistry and habitability.
objects.firstPerson: I carried four sealed beakers of Earth water to Mars. When we mixed in the red arctic dirt, my ion electrodes tasted the broth: mildly alkaline, rich in magnesium, potassium, and perchlorate salts. The soil of Mars was chemically alive.

objects.name: Dual Decagonal Bio-Solar Arrays
objects.description: Twin fan-folding decagonal solar panels spanning 5.52 metres that unfolded like oriental fans after landing. In peak summer they produced 3.5 kWh daily under 24-hour midnight sun.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Demonstrated the power profile of circular fan-fold arrays, paving the way for the UltraFlex arrays deployed on the InSight and Lucy spacecraft.
objects.legacy: Collapsed under hundreds of kilograms of dry-ice (CO2) frost during the brutal 2008–2009 polar winter, seen in HiRISE orbital images.
objects.firstPerson: I fanned open like black silk wings under the arctic sun that never set. Day after day, I drank the midnight sunlight to feed our heaters and pumps. But as winter crept in, the sun slipped below the icy hills, and heavy dry-ice snow folded me forever.

objects.name: MET Weather Station & Laser Lidar
objects.description: Canadian Space Agency meteorological station with temperature and pressure sensors and a dual-wavelength neodymium-YAG laser lidar that fired green pulses 20 kilometres up into the arctic atmosphere.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Observed water-ice clouds 4 km high and directly detected snow falling from Martian clouds, sublimating before reaching the ground (virga).
objects.legacy: Proved that precipitation and active hydrological cycles exist in the contemporary Martian atmosphere.
objects.firstPerson: I fired emerald laser beams into the purple arctic sky. Night after night, the scattered light told me a magical secret: four kilometers above my deck, water-ice crystals were clumping into snowflakes and drifting downward toward the plain.
